hints: Think about what volatility really means, how easily molecules escape from liquid to gas, and which forces have to be broken to do that.
Remember that $\text{Cl}_2$, $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ are all simple non-polar molecules, so identify the only intermolecular force acting between them.
Connect the strength of that intermolecular force to what increases down the group, more electrons giving larger temporary dipoles, and see which option matches.
walkthrough:
**Understand volatility**

Volatility tells us how easily a liquid turns into a gas. Low volatility means a high boiling point, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

To boil, we break intermolecular forces between molecules, not covalent bonds within molecules.

**Identify the forces between halogen molecules**

Chlorine, bromine and iodine exist as diatomic molecules: $\text{Cl}_2$, $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$. They are non-polar, so the only forces between molecules are London (induced dipole-dipole) forces.

**Link London forces to electrons down the group**

London forces get stronger when there are more electrons, because the electron cloud is larger and more easily polarised to form temporary dipoles.

Down Group 17: $\text{Cl}$ (17 electrons) < $\text{Br}$ (35 electrons) < $\text{I}$ (53 electrons), so forces get stronger, boiling point rises, and volatility decreases.

**Choose the responsible factor**

Bond length, bond strength and electronegativity describe what happens inside the atom or molecule. They do not control boiling.

The number of electrons controls the strength of London forces between molecules, so this explains the volatility trend.

options.A: Bond length does increase down the group, but it describes the covalent bond inside the $\text{X}_2$ molecule. Boiling does not break this bond, so it does not control volatility.
options.B: Bond strength describes how hard it is to break the covalent $\text{X-X}$ bond. Volatility only requires breaking weak London forces between molecules, so covalent bond strength is irrelevant here.
options.C: Electronegativity decreases down the group, but all three halogens form non-polar molecules with London forces only. Electronegativity does not determine the strength of these forces.
options.D: Correct. More electrons down the group means a larger, more polarisable electron cloud. This gives stronger London forces between $\text{Cl}_2$, $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ molecules, higher boiling points and lower volatility.
